title: Redwood Discovery - Lyra Systems latency & throughput
next_steps: Send latency/throughput benchmark template and onboarding doc
Share security pack (SOC2/KMS/SSO) and private deployment checklist
Schedule micro-benchmark run next week with Lyra test corpus
action_items: Samir: prepare dedicated vs hosted config and rough cost delta by 2027-07-08
Marcus: provide representative token/sec distribution and p95 targets by 2027-07-06
summary: Discovery focused on p95 latency targets, concurrency requirements, streaming behavior, and token/sec benchmarking across Redwood hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Security and data residency discussed; customer looking to pilot Dedicated with option to move Private for regulated workloads.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-07-05 14:00 PDT | Duration: 48 mins | Attendees: Avery Chen, Samir Patel - Redwood; Dana Kline, Marcus Liu, Priya Menon - Lyra Systems

[00:00] Avery: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Avery from Redwood, can you hear me okay?
[00:05] Dana: Yep, loud and clear. Thanks for setting this up.
[00:08] Samir: Hi all, Samir on the engineering side. We'll focus on latency/throughput and how to meet your p95 targets.
[00:15] Dana: Great. To give context, Lyra runs real-time code assistant features inside our IDE. Target p95 for prompt-to-first-token is 250ms for short completions (~20-50 tokens), and for longer streaming completions we'd like sub-500ms p95 for initial token and then sustain streaming at ~50-70 tokens/sec aggregate per connection.
[00:40] Marcus: Concurrency: we expect bursts up to 400 concurrent user sessions during peak -- average sustained concurrency maybe 120. Token/sec distribution attached in the doc but I can summarize: about 60% of requests are short sync completions, 30% are streaming sessions 30-200 tokens, 10% are long batch/finetune-ish calls.
[01:05] Samir: Okay that helps. Are you considering Redwood hosted, dedicated reserved capacity, or a private VPC/on-prem setup?
[01:12] Dana: Initially hosted or dedicated; we might move to Private later because of EU data residency and a handful of enterprise customers with strict KMS/HSM requirements. Cost is a factor but latency and reliability are non-negotiable.
[01:25] Priya: From security side, we need SOC2, SSO/SAML with SCIM, audit logs retention for 12 months, and customer-managed keys (KMS) for Private. Also need to understand data retention on hosted.
[01:40] Avery: We can definitely provide SOC2 docs and SSO/SAML with SCIM; hosted has configurable retention and we offer Dedicated with optional private control plane. For KMS, Private gives you full customer-managed keys; in Dedicated we can integrate with customer KMS in many cases, we'll send specifics.
[01:55] Marcus: On the perf side, what's typical p95 on hosted for a model like small-llama-13b quantized, and what delta do you see moving to Dedicated?
[02:05] Samir: Roughly speaking, hosted p95 for short prompts on optimized 8-bit quant models is around 200-350ms depending on seq length and network hop. Dedicated on colocated GPUs with pinned instances reduces variability and can shave 30-60ms p95 and improves stability under concurrency. Those are ballpark numbers — we should run a micro-benchmark with your payload to be precise.
[02:30] Dana: That variability worries us — our users notice jitter. How much does streaming help versus chunking? We need steady early token p95.
[02:38] Samir: Streaming semantics matter. We support chunked streaming and can control prefix caching to lower repeated prefix cost. For initial token latency, warm KV cache and batching policy matter; we can pin models on Dedicated pools to keep warm caches. In Hosted warmup helps but eviction during spikes causes spikes.
[02:58] Marcus: For benchmarking, what metrics should we capture? We're collecting p50/p95/p99 latency, cold vs warm starts, tokens/sec, connection churn, and tail latency under concurrency. Anything else?
[03:10] Samir: Also measure tokens per second per GPU, effective throughput with your batch sizes, and streaming throughput per connection. Capture model variants (quantization bitwidth), sequence length distribution, and network RTT from your region to our hosted region. We'll provide a benchmark spreadsheet.
[03:26] Dana: Perfect. On scale: at 400 concurrent users and say average 40 tokens per streaming session, what tokens/sec aggregate should we expect?
[03:33] Marcus: Quick math: 400 concurrent * 40 tokens = 16k tokens in flight; if each connection streams 50 tokens/sec ideally that's 20k tokens/sec aggregate. We need to know GPU tokens/sec so we can capacity plan.
[03:46] Samir: For quantized 13B on an A100-ish equivalent, you might see roughly 15-30k tokens/sec per GPU depending on context/window and optimizations; high throughput rigs or LLM-specialized inference hardware improves that. We'll run exact numbers with your test set.
[04:05] Priya: What's the mitigation for noisy neighbors in Hosted? Our SLAs in enterprise customers require predictable p95.
[04:10] Avery: Dedicated gives you isolated GPU pools and configurable autoscaling policies. We also support reservation and burst packs. Hosted uses multi-tenant pooling but with performance profiles; for strict p95 SLOs we usually recommend Dedicated or Private.
[04:25] Dana: For Private, do you support air-gapped on-prem? We have one customer who might require that later.
[04:30] Avery: Yes, Private supports on-prem packaged deployment; the control plane can be customer-managed in a VPC. There are additional ops responsibilities and integration steps. We'll include the checklist.
[04:40] Marcus: Regarding tokenization differences — sometimes our token counts differ from your benchmarks. How do we align?
[04:44] Samir: We'll run your actual tokenizer and prompt set against the models we test. Token/sec depends heavily on prompt length and dynamic KV reuse. Also streaming chunk sizing changes apparent tokens/sec.
[04:55] Dana: For the pilot, we want: 1) p95 < 250ms for short completions; 2) streaming steady-state at ~50 tokens/sec per connection; 3) capacity planning for 20k-30k tokens/sec aggregate. Can Redwood provide a recommended Dedicated config to meet those?
[05:12] Samir: Yes, we'll propose node counts, instance types, and batching configs. Expect suggested Dedicated profile plus Hosted fallback for burst. We'll include quantization recommendation (8-bit or 4-bit) and whether to enable KV cache pinning to hit p95.
[05:28] Marcus: Cost delta is important — can you give rough monthly estimates?
[05:31] Avery: We'll provide a TCO slide: reserved Dedicated monthly cost vs Hosted pay-as-you-go. Ballpark: Dedicated commit reduces per-token cost by 30-60% depending on utilization, but we'll give specific numbers after we pick model and instance types.
[05:48] Priya: Security detail: in Hosted where is data-at-rest encrypted, and how do we manage deletion requests?
[05:53] Avery: Hosted encrypts at rest and in transit; we can support stricter retention policies and deletion workflows via API. For regulated volumes we recommend Private or Dedicated with customer-controlled keys. We'll attach SOC2 and retention docs.
[06:08] Marcus: On benchmarking cadence: we should run a quick micro-benchmark with a 1k request sample, then follow with a 10k mixed workload. How long to schedule and what do you need from us?
[06:18] Samir: For the micro-run we just need your prompt corpus (anonymized), token distribution, target seq lengths, and a test client IP/region. We can run within 3 business days once we have that. For larger runs we'll coordinate time slots to avoid noisy windows.
[06:34] Dana: Can Redwood stream to partial outputs so we can start rendering tokens in our UI? Latency to first byte matters more than completion.
[06:40] Samir: Yes, we support streaming responses with chunked delivery and webhooks or websockets; you can get the first token quickly if model is warmed and you use smaller initial chunk sizes. We'll show recommended chunking parameters.
[06:55] Marcus: Any notes about failover? If Dedicated pool has an outage can requests fail over to Hosted model variants?
[07:00] Avery: We support smart routing and automatic fallback policies; you can configure canary A/B and fallback to hosted variants. We'll document RTO/RPO expectations.
[07:10] Dana: Great. One concern: tail p99s spike due to cold KV cache misses. Can you describe mitigation?
[07:16] Samir: Warmup strategies: pre-warming KV caches, model pinning, and prefix caching. Also adaptive batching to reduce per-token overhead. We'll test with your workload to tune.
[07:30] Marcus: For our evaluation, how do we interpret tokens/sec per GPU vs effective tokens served to users? Example: if you show 20k tokens/sec per GPU raw but with batching of many sessions the effective throughput is different.
[07:40] Samir: Good callout. Raw tokens/sec is hardware throughput; effective tokens/sec accounts for per-request overhead, batching inefficiency, network RTT, and streaming chunking. We'll provide both raw and effective metrics from our runs.
[07:55] Priya: Will you supply an architecture diagram for Dedicated and Private? We need to show it to the security review board.
[07:59] Avery: Yes we'll include architecture diagrams, network flow, and SAML/KMS integrations in the security pack.
[08:08] Dana: Okay let's recap next steps.
[08:12] Avery: Recap: 1) Redwood sends benchmark spreadsheet and security pack (SOC2, SSO/KMS docs). 2) Lyra shares anonymized prompt corpus, token distribution, and target p95 SLOs. 3) Redwood schedules micro-benchmark and provides Dedicated sizing recommendation and cost estimate.
[08:26] Marcus: Sounds good. Tentatively schedule benchmark run for next Thursday? I'll confirm after I send the corpus.
[08:33] Priya: I'll follow up with questions on retention and key management if anything else comes up.
[08:38] Avery: Great thanks everyone. We'll send materials by EOD tomorrow.
[08:42] Dana: Thanks all, talk soon.

End transcript.

Notes about transcription: occasional mis-IDs of speakers, some technical terms slightly garbled (KV cache sometimes transcribed as K-V cash), small filler words present.
